section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Projection Intuition
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as arrows. Introduce the dot product as the product of the length of one vector and the shadow (projection) cast by the other vector onto it. This transforms a 2D interaction into a 1D scalar value.
section_1.example: Visualize a flashlight shining on a needle (vector v) resting on a table (vector w). The shadow length on the table represents the dot product.

section_2.title: Defining Duality: The Linear Functional
section_2.content: Explain that a dot product with a fixed vector 'w' is a machine that takes an input vector 'v' and outputs a scalar. This 'machine' is a linear functional. Duality states that every linear transformation from vectors to scalars is just a dot product in disguise.
section_2.example: Think of 'w' as a 'filter' or 'gatekeeper'. If 'w' is a weight vector, the dot product calculates the 'total score' of a set of features (vector 'v').

section_3.title: Visualizing the Dual Space
section_3.content: Instead of arrows, represent the dot product result as a set of parallel lines (level sets). The vector 'w' defines the direction of the lines, and the dot product tells us which 'line' the input 'v' lands on.
section_3.example: Use a topographic map: the vector 'w' points uphill, and the contour lines represent constant dot product values. Any vector 'v' landing on the same contour line has the same dot product with 'w'.

section_4.title: Synthesis: The Power of Perspective
section_4.content: Conclude by showing how duality allows us to bridge geometry (the vector) and algebra (the functional). Emphasize that the dot product is the bridge that turns geometry into calculation.
section_4.example: A robotic arm (vector 'v') sensing a pressure field (defined by 'w'). The dot product calculates the total torque applied to the joint, showing how geometry informs physics.

    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Projection Intuition
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as arrows. Introduce the dot product as the product of the length of one vector and the shadow (projection) cast by the other vector onto it. This transforms a 2D interaction into a 1D scalar value.
section_1.example: Visualize a flashlight shining on a needle (vector v) resting on a table (vector w). The shadow length on the table represents the dot product.

section_2.title: Defining Duality: The Linear Functional
section_2.content: Explain that a dot product with a fixed vector 'w' is a machine that takes an input vector 'v' and outputs a scalar. This 'machine' is a linear functional. Duality states that every linear transformation from vectors to scalars is just a dot product in disguise.
section_2.example: Think of 'w' as a 'filter' or 'gatekeeper'. If 'w' is a weight vector, the dot product calculates the 'total score' of a set of features (vector 'v').

section_3.title: Visualizing the Dual Space
section_3.content: Instead of arrows, represent the dot product result as a set of parallel lines (level sets). The vector 'w' defines the direction of the lines, and the dot product tells us which 'line' the input 'v' lands on.
section_3.example: Use a topographic map: the vector 'w' points uphill, and the contour lines represent constant dot product values. Any vector 'v' landing on the same contour line has the same dot product with 'w'.

section_4.title: Synthesis: The Power of Perspective
section_4.content: Conclude by showing how duality allows us to bridge geometry (the vector) and algebra (the functional). Emphasize that the dot product is the bridge that turns geometry into calculation.
section_4.example: A robotic arm (vector 'v') sensing a pressure field (defined by 'w'). The dot product calculates the total torque applied to the joint, showing how geometry informs physics.
